candidates.attacker_control: Content of an untrusted XML Schema file (e.g. a poisoned .xsd in a cloned repository or a schema downloaded from an untrusted source) that the developer opens. The attacker controls DOCTYPE/DTD declarations and entity declarations inside the schema text, including SYSTEM identifiers pointing at file: URIs, internal network hosts, or attacker servers. No server-side privilege is needed; the malicious document is ordinary workspace content.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: Checked the XML document validation path: LSPXMLParserConfiguration.java:63-70 correctly maps both features to validationSettings (default false), showing the intended security posture and that the XSD path is inconsistent with it. Checked XMLValidationSettings defaults (false/false) and that these settings are consumed nowhere else (only LSPXMLParserConfiguration). Checked that the XSD diagnostics participant is registered by default and only asserts DOMUtils.isXSD. Checked that the resolver installed is the full URI resolver chain, not a file-restricted one. Checked the other XML parsers in the codebase (DOMUtils.newSAXParserFactory sets disallow-doctype-decl true; XSDAnnotationModel/DataType/AssociateGrammarCommand use it) and found no other unconditional external-entity enablement. Considered that the literal true values could be intentional support for entity references inside schema documents, but no comment or setting documents that, and the sibling SAX path was explicitly hardened against XXE in 0.18.1 (CHANGELOG #1104).
candidates.impact: With default settings, opening a malicious XSD causes the language server to (1) make outbound HTTP/HTTPS/FTP requests to attacker-chosen URLs, including internal/loopback services and cloud metadata endpoints reachable from the developer's machine (SSRF), (2) read and expand local files via file: entity/DTD identifiers, with expanded content entering the schema model and potentially the editor UI (hover/documentation) and error messages, and (3) expose the server to entity-expansion/external-fetch resource exhaustion. The explicit user settings disallowDocTypeDecl/resolveExternalEntities (default false) are silently bypassed for XSD documents, defeating an existing security control.
candidates.prerequisites: The LemMinX server is running with default settings (XMLValidationSettings defaults: enabled=true, disallowDocTypeDecl=false, resolveExternalEntities=false) and the user opens an .xsd file (or a file whose root element is bound to http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema, see DOMUtils.isXSD / XSDDiagnosticsParticipant.java:43) so that XSDDiagnosticsParticipant invokes XSDValidator. The XSD contains a DOCTYPE with an external DTD/entity or an external parameter entity reference. Because this path ignores resolveExternalEntities/disallowDocTypeDecl, the user's hardening settings do not prevent resolution.
candidates.root_cause: XSDValidator.doDiagnostics builds an XMLGrammarPreparser for validating XSD files and explicitly enables 'http://xml.org/sax/features/external-general-entities' and 'http://xml.org/sax/features/external-parameter-entities' with the literal value true (XSDValidator.java:81-84). validationSettings is only consulted for isRelatedInformation() (XSDValidator.java:62-64), so the user-facing XMLValidationSettings.resolveExternalEntities and disallowDocTypeDecl flags (defaults false; XMLValidationSettings.java:29-31,43-50) are never applied on this path, unlike the XML-document parser configuration (LSPXMLParserConfiguration.java:63-70). The document's full entity resolver (URIResolverExtensionManager, incl. file: and http/https/ftp download-to-cache via XMLCacheResolverExtension) is installed on the preparser (XSDValidator.java:94-96), so attacker-declared SYSTEM entities/DTDs in the schema are resolved.
candidates.title: Unconditional external entity resolution in XSD validation (XXE / external entity expansion bypasses validation settings)
candidates.trace: XSDPlugin registers XSDDiagnosticsParticipant (XSDPlugin.java:64,96) -> XMLDiagnostics.doExtensionsDiagnostics runs all diagnostics participants when validation is enabled (XMLDiagnostics.java:60-73) -> XSDDiagnosticsParticipant.doDiagnostics checks DOMUtils.isXSD(xmlDocument) and then calls XSDValidator.doDiagnostics with the document's resolver manager wrapped in LSPXMLEntityResolver (XSDDiagnosticsParticipant.java:43-55) -> XSDValidator sets EXTERNAL_GENERAL_ENTITIES_FEATURE=true and EXTERNAL_PARAMETER_ENTITIES_FEATURE=true on the grammar preparser (XSDValidator.java:81-84), regardless of validationSettings, and installs the resolver (XSDValidator.java:94-96) -> the schema text (document.getText()) is parsed by the schema loader (XSDValidator.java:98-103), so SYSTEM entities/external DTD subsets in the attacker's XSD are resolved through URIResolverExtensionManager.resolveEntity (line 120-130) -> for http(s)/ftp the XMLCacheResolverExtension downloads the resource into the ~/.lemminx cache and returns it (XMLCacheResolverExtension.java:73-103); for file: the default resolver returns the local path. Entity-expanded text can additionally surface through the schema content model (XSDAnnotationModel parses xs:documentation/appinfo and exposes it in hover/completion).
candidates.unverified: Not runtime-confirmed and not executed: the Xerces-J 2.12.2 dependency jar is not part of the snapshot, so I could not verify (a) that XMLGrammarPreparser.setFeature propagates these two features to the already-registered XMLSchemaLoader at preparseGrammar time, nor (b) exact expansion behavior. No network/file-system testing was performed, and no end-to-end exploit was attempted. Also unverified: whether upstream LemMinX intentionally left this path entity-enabled (the code contains no comment justifying it).
candidates.weakness_type: CWE-611 Improper Restriction of XML External Entity Reference (XXE); also CWE-918-adjacent SSRF

coverage_summary: Scope: get_source_scope reports 442 visible files (404 Java, 0 omitted/symlinked/sensitive-name exclusions) in a single module, version 0.18.5-SNAPSHOT; binary-like files are skipped for reading. get_relation_scope reports a complete syntax index (4526 symbols, 11080 calls) with no semantic resolution, no control/data flow, and unresolved calls (6009) — all index results were treated as navigation hints and verified against source. I reviewed the trust boundary from LSP entry points (XMLTextDocumentService/XMLWorkspaceService/commands) through diagnostics (XMLDiagnostics, ContentModelDiagnosticsParticipant, XSDDiagnosticsParticipant, DTDDiagnosticsParticipant), the Xerces integration (LSPXMLParserConfiguration, LSPSAXParser, XMLValidator, XSDValidator, DTDValidator, ExternalXMLDTDValidator, XMLModelHandler), content-model loading and caching (ContentModelManager, CacheResourcesManager, XMLCacheResolverExtension, XSD/XSL/catalog resolvers, FilesUtils), and representative DOM/parser utilities. My coverage is not exhaustive: large service/util files (XMLCompletions, XMLPositionUtility, XMLFormatter, XMLRename, XMLScanner details beyond spot checks), generators, entities/references/prolog/xsi extensions, telemetry/settings serialization, and the exact behavior of the Xerces/lsp4j/Guava dependencies (jars not in snapshot) were not fully reviewed or verified.
limitations: No code execution, tests, scanners, or exploit payloads were run; all conclusions are static and source-based.
Dependency jars (Xerces 2.12.2, lsp4j, Guava, jsoup) are not part of the snapshot, so parser feature propagation, URI normalization, and runtime library behavior could not be verified.

The repository snapshot contains no tests, build outputs, git history, or patch data, so I could not confirm whether the XSD external-entity enablement is upstream intentional code or an introduced deviation.
Severity/exploitability statements are limited to source-level reasoning; the selected candidate was not runtime-confirmed and remains a lead.
Large parts of the 442-file tree were sampled rather than read line-by-line; coverage limitations above list the main unreviewed areas.

rejected_leads.lead: ContentModelManager.evictCacheFor deletes files without a cache-containment check (ContentModelManager.java:434-441: Files.deleteIfExists(FilesUtils.getPath(resolvedURI))), while the sibling download path is guarded by FilesUtils.isIncludedInDeployedPath (CacheResourcesManager.java:150). A crafted xsi:noNamespaceSchemaLocation whose URI path contains dot-segments/percent-encoded dot-segments could make getResourceCachePath (CacheResourcesManager.java:244-248) compute a path outside ~/.lemminx, yielding arbitrary file deletion when the client invokes the xml.validation.current.file command (XMLValidationFileCommand.java:52-62).
rejected_leads.reason: Rejected as the primary candidate because exploitability depends on unverified behavior outside the snapshot: whether Xerces' XMLEntityManager.expandSystemId (dependency jar not included) preserves literal or %2e%2e-encoded dot segments in the resolved URI, and whether FilesUtils.getPath/Path.toUri preserve them; additionally it requires the user to explicitly trigger the revalidation command. Evidence remains strong enough to note, but it is weaker end-to-end than the XSD entity issue.

rejected_leads.lead: URIResolverExtensionManager.unregisterResolver adds the resolver to the list instead of removing it (URIResolverExtensionManager.java:91-93: resolvers.add(resolver)) while its javadoc says 'Unregister an URI resolver' and every sibling unregister* method uses remove (e.g. XMLExtensionsRegistry.unregisterCompletionParticipant:296-298, XMLWorkspaceService.unregisterCommand:114-118).
rejected_leads.reason: Looks like a copy/paste defect (state accumulation/stale resolvers after plugin stop), but the direct security impact is weak: it does not create a new attacker-controlled data flow, and it only affects resolver lifecycle. Not selected.

rejected_leads.lead: CacheResourcesManager.downloadResource follows Location headers to arbitrary URLs when redirects are handled manually (CacheResourcesManager.java:193-200), potentially reaching file: URLs.
rejected_leads.reason: Unverified and likely mitigated: HttpURLConnection follows redirects itself by default, so the manual loop generally does not execute, and any downloaded content is written only to the computed cache path. Not selected.

rejected_leads.lead: XSDValidator/DTDValidator/CMDTDDocument do not configure a Xerces SecurityManager/entity-expansion limit, unlike LSPXMLParserConfiguration (lines 71-77).
rejected_leads.reason: Plausible DoS hardening gap, but its effect depends on Xerces 2.12.2 defaults/security-manager installation semantics that cannot be verified from the snapshot; secondary to the selected candidate.

summary: Reviewed the Eclipse LemMinX snapshot (442 files, 404 Java files; version 0.18.5-SNAPSHOT). I traced the untrusted-XML trust boundary (document/XSD content -> Xerces validators -> URI/entity resolvers -> filesystem/network). Strongest source-backed issue: the XSD validation path unconditionally re-enables external general/parameter entity resolution for the Xerces grammar preparser, ignoring the server's own resolveExternalEntities / disallowDocTypeDecl settings (which default to false and are honored only in the XML-document SAX path). A malicious .xsd opened in the workspace therefore triggers external entity resolution (local file access and outbound http/https/ftp requests through the LemMinX resolver/cache chain) with default settings. Other leads (missing cache-containment check before deleting a computed cache path; unregisterResolver adding instead of removing) are listed as rejected/unconfirmed.
